newsitem.title: UK: WEEK AHEAD - Markets to pounce on inflation data.
newsitem.headline: WEEK AHEAD - Markets to pounce on inflation data.

text.p: Financial markets will train their sights firmly on inflation data from the United States and Europe in the week ahead, economists and analysts said.
The data should not hold any terrors for the markets, particularly after a stunning drop in U.S. payrolls on Friday, they said. Debt markets, notably high yielders, will rally on.

"If the Treasury market is going to roll then Europe is going to roll and if Europe is going to roll then people are going to continue to look at the high yielders," said Stuart Thomson, chief international economist at Nikko Securities here.
Top of the list will be U.S. September producer prices and retail sales on Friday.

If the figures are weak, the yield on the Treasury long bond may be able to carve out a new lower range, said Thomson. He sees it edging to a 6.50-6.80 percent range from the 6.80-7.13 percent area it has been locked in since April.

"A weak employment report coupled with reasonable producer price figures and the market will have established this new range for the time being, particularly as it appears there is continued moderate growth on retail sales," he said.

Robert Prior, international economist at HSBC James Capel in London, sees producer prices up 0.1 percent in September, down from a 0.3 percent gain in August. He expects retail sales to be flat on August's 0.1 percent gain, reflecting weak auto sales.

Inflation data from Europe will also be flooding in, with Britain, France, Portugal, Sweden, The Netherlands and Spain all set to release figures, said Keith Edmonds, chief analyst at IBJ International in London.

"All these data are going to show a very benign future for inflation across Europe... and although we may not see any further rate cuts in the core, there is still scope for rate reductions elsewhere," he said.
Inflation data for the UK comes in the form of September retail prices on Thursday. France releases September consumer price data on Friday.

"The UK RPI (retail price index) will likely fall back reasonably sharply to around 1.9 percent year-on-year and so that could raise the spectre of an interest rate cut," said Prior. In August, the British RPI grew an annual 2.1 percent.
Optimism over European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) should remain a dominant theme in Europe, with high yielding bonds and currencies converging further on core European markets, analysts said.
British markets should continue to ride the wave, though the Conservative Party conference in Bournemouth, England over the week is unlikely to produce much of a boost on the EMU front, Edmonds said.
Any statements from the ruling Conservatives will only serve to underline the difference between ambiguous British policy and recent commitments from other European countries, Edmonds said.
German unemployment will receive attention on Tuesday, with September data due and a press conference from the trendsetting IG Metall union about their 1997 wage demands.
"Employment and the impact on Germany is going to be key on Tuesday," said Thomson. He said the data will show employment continuing to creep up.
He forecasts a seasonally adjusted gain of 10,000 in German payrolls in September after a 14,000 gain in September.
Japan will also release important data, the bulk of it on Tuesday with August current account and trade data, August machinery orders and September wholesale prices due.
And finally, economists everywhere should dust off their dinner jackets. The Nobel prize for economics is announced on Tuesday.
